Sample text:
---
At four in the morning, a city belongs to water pipes, distant freight trains, and people who have made a quiet peace with the dark.

Inside the bakery on Elm Street, the only light comes from the hooded bulbs over the maple worktable and the amber glow bleeding through the oven glass. Outside, the streetlamp at the corner hums to itself, casting a pale cone over wet asphalt. It rained sometime around midnight, the kind of cold October rain that strips the last stubborn leaves from the sycamores and plasters them flat against the curb.

Julian ties his apron—canvas, stiff at the hems, dusted permanently into the weave with rye flour—and checks the thermometer on the proof box. Seventy-eight degrees. A small, tropical climate held inside sheet metal while the rest of the neighborhood shivers at forty-one.

There is a particular relief to working before the world starts asking questions. At noon, everything has an edge: the register chimes, the espresso wand hisses, people lean over the counter with half-formed apologies and hurried orders, looking at their watches while they ask for sourdough. At four, there is only mass, temperature, and time.

He pulls the first tub of dough from the retarder. It has been sleeping since yesterday afternoon, fermenting slowly in the cold, turning simple flour and water into something faintly sharp, almost like green apples and wet grain. When he tips the tub onto the floured maple, the dough releases with a soft *shhh* and spreads slowly, heavy and alive.

His hands know the geometry before he thinks about it. Bench scraper, fold, turn, tuck. The skin of the dough tightens beneath the heels of his palms until it turns smooth and taut, holding its own breath. Forty loaves, lined up in linen-lined baskets like sleeping animals.

Across the room, the deck oven clicks. Its heating elements have reached five hundred degrees, and the iron radiates a dry, enveloping heat that settles right behind his eyes. He remembers his grandfather’s workshop—not a bakery, a small room behind a garage where the old man repaired radios—carrying that same smell of hot dust and quiet patience. People rarely appreciate how much of any craft is just waiting for heat to do what you cannot force with your hands.

Around five-fifteen, someone pauses outside the front window.

Julian looks up, a lame blade resting between his thumb and forefinger. Under the awning, just beyond the glare of the interior lights, stands a woman in a navy wool coat, a canvas tote slung over one shoulder. Maybe a nurse coming off the night shift at St. Jude’s three blocks up; maybe a janitor heading home before the buses get crowded. She isn’t looking at the door—the *Closed* sign is still turned toward the street—she is just standing close to the glass, palms tucked into her coat pockets, soaking in the faint ghost of warmth radiating through the pane.

Julian lifts a hand in a small, uncertain wave. She nods once, her breath fogging a silver dollar of condensation onto the window, and then walks on toward the bus shelter at the end of the block. The fog disappears in three seconds, leaving the glass dark again.

He turns back to the peel. Scoring the loaves requires commitment; hesitate with the razor and the blade drags, tearing the skin instead of parting it cleanly. One swift arc across the top of each boule, just deep enough to give the trapped steam somewhere to escape. He slides them onto the hearth stone, throws a cup of ice cubes onto the cast-iron tray beneath to flood the chamber with steam, and shuts the heavy door.

In the quiet that follows, he sweeps the bench. Flour gathers in drifts along the backsplash, soft as chalk. It is strange, he thinks sometimes, to spend five hours every morning building something designed to be torn apart and gone by dinner. Nothing he makes lasts forty-eight hours. There are no monuments in a bakery, no shelves of old work to admire ten years later. Only a rhythm: mix, ferment, bake, sell, sweep. Tomorrow the table will be bare again, waiting for the exact same gestures.

Yet when the timer chimes and he pulls the first batch onto the cooling racks, he never quite believes it’s ordinary.

The loaves come out the color of old chestnuts, blistered along the scored ears, dark mahogany where the heat kissed the edges. As the cool air of the room hits them, the crusts begin to sing—tiny, sharp fractures opening across the surface like thin ice settling on a pond. *Tick, tick, crackle.* If you stand very still beside the rack, you can hear an entire choir of cooling bread whispering to itself.

By six-thirty, the sky behind the brick rowhouses across the street has thinned from black to slate blue. A delivery truck rumbles past, its headlights sweeping across the tin ceiling and vanishing. Up on the corner, the streetlamp flickers once and gives up for the day.

Julian washes the flour from his forearms at the deep steel sink, dries his hands on a striped towel, and walks to the front of the shop. He flips the latch, swings the door open just an inch to let the sharp morning air spill over the threshold, and turns the sign in the window.

The bell above the door gives a tiny, brass tremor. Somewhere down the street, footsteps start coming closer.
---
